newsitem.title: CANADA: Toronto stocks set 17th record close of 1997.
newsitem.headline: Toronto stocks set 17th record close of 1997.

text.p: Toronto's key stock index posted its 17th record close of the year on Thursday as U.S. inflation concerns eased, boosting banks and interest-sensitive sectors.
The broader market ended mixed as influential gold issues slipped on weaker bullion prices. Declining issues edged out advancers 488 to 472, while 328 traded flat.
The Toronto Stock Exchange's 300 Composite Index rose 56.10 points to close at 6515.61.
Yorkton Securities trader Pier Donnini said investors cheered lower than expected U.S. retail sales for May.
May figures dipped 0.1 percent, contrary to economists' forecasts of a 0.4 percent gain.
Donnini said market players had few investment options other than equities as the chance of a U.S. interest-rate hike decreased, keeping returns on bonds low.
Turnover was active at 90.2 million shares worth C$1.5 billion ($1.1 billion).
New York soared for a fifth straight day, vaulting over the 7700 level with a jump of 136 points.
"It doesn't seem to want to stop. We're floating on air," Donnini said.
Canada's bond market also rallied, with the 30-year bond yield dropping below its U.S. counterpart for the first time ever, analysts said.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$1.72 to yield 6.753 percent, while the U.S. 30-year bond yield reached 6.77 percent, creating a negative spread of two basis points between the two.
All of Toronto's 14 sub-indexes gained, except for golds. Media issues led the charge, followed by heavyweight banks, utilities and transportation.
Among individual issues, banks posted impressive gains, including Royal Bank of Canada, which climbed 1.40 to 60.30 and Toronto-Dominion Bank, up 1.30 to 42.70.

Vehicle parts maker Magna International Inc. gained 5.10 to 81.30 after reporting strong third-quarter numbers on Wednesday. Earnings rose to C$1.60 a share for the quarter ended April 30 from year earlier C$1.33.
